newsitem.title: UK: No sign of lower air fares despite cheaper fuel.
newsitem.headline: No sign of lower air fares despite cheaper fuel.

text.p: Air travellers are getting a raw deal from big airlines who have failed to slash ticket prices despite lower jet fuel costs although cargo fares have come down, consumer groups say.
"Unfortunately it's no surprise - the cargo shippers are in a better position to negotiate," said Phil Evans of Britain's Consumer Association.

"There is no real reason why air fares shouldn't come down if cargo surcharges have been cut, but the average air passenger is probably unaware of the price of jet fuel, unlike cargo shippers," he added.

European jet fuel has fallen 32 percent since the beginning of the year and while a large number of airlines have cut the prices they charge to carry cargo, they have steadfastly maintained the level of air fares.

When jet aviation fuel prices started to climb last year, the industry was quick to react since fuel accounts for around 15 percent of an airline's operating cost. Air fares were increased by up to three percent and surcharges applied to cargoes.
Since the beginning of April the number of airlines that have dropped the cargo surcharge has risen steadily. One of the latest last week was British Airways, one of the world's largest airlines.
But, none of the major airlines has reduced the prices of tickets individual travellers have to pay.

"The lowering of the price of jet fuel is not significant enough to offer a change in fare structure," a British Airways spokesman said on Tuesday. "Fuel is just one of the many cost factors of an airline".
Back in October 1996 a company spokesman told Reuters: "We have been forced to file a number of fare increases recently, primarily as a result of the leaping cost of aviation fuel."
The price of a delivered tonne of jet fuel was around $282 a tonne in early October 1996 compared with a price today of about $190. In April last year prices were around $195 a tonne.

Airlines cite the stronger dollar which makes fuel more expensive for European operators and high non-fuel operating costs as reasons why airfares have not been cut. But consumer groups say this argument does not hold up given the cuts in cargo surcharges.
"If they can cut cargo surcharges, why can't they also cut air fares?" asked the Consumer Association's Evans.
Airline executives say it is unlikely air fares will be cut because of the lower fuel prices.
"Airlines will hold on to whatever gains they have made to offset high operating costs. Jet prices rose (in 1996) by about 40 percent but fares were only increased by about three percent," said one.

"The dropping of cargo surcharges is more related to empty cargo holds rather than lower fuel prices. The only way fares (for passengers) will fall is if there are empty seats," said an industry executive who did not want to be named.
